q: How does the final ‹de› in ‹cidade› sound in most of Brazil?
why: ‹t› and ‹d› before an ee sound turn into ch and j, and a final ‹e› sounds ee, so ‹de› sounds jee.

q: Where is the stress in ‹falar› (to speak)?
why: ‹falar› ends in ‹r›, not in ‹a›, ‹e›, ‹o›, ‹am›, ‹em› or ‹ens›, so the stress falls on the last syllable: fah-LAHR.

q: What does the tilde in ‹pão› tell you?
o: The vowel goes through the nose
The stress is on the first letter
why: A tilde marks a nasal vowel: ‹pão› (bread) is nasal, ‹pau› (stick) is not.

q: A woman thanks a man. What does she say?
why: ‹obrigada› agrees with the speaker, and the speaker is a woman.

q: It's 3 p.m. How do you greet someone?
why: After about noon it is ‹boa tarde›, and ‹boa› is feminine because ‹tarde› is.

q: You meet your friend's grandmother. Which 'you' fits best?
why: ‹a senhora› is the respectful 'you' for an older woman; ‹o senhor› is for a man.
‹problema› ends in ‹-a› but is masculine: ‹o problema›.
‹água› is feminine, so 'a' is ‹uma›; ‹a água› means the water.

q: What is the plural of ‹o limão›?
why: Many ‹-ão› nouns change to ‹-ões›, and the article goes plural too: ‹os limões›.
‹você› takes the ‹ele› form: ‹você é›.
No article before a job, and ‹professora› agrees with the speaker, a woman.

q: Which form of ‹ser› goes with ‹a gente›?
why: ‹a gente› takes the ‹ele› form: ‹a gente é›.
‹irmãs› is feminine and plural, so the article and the adjective agree: ‹as irmãs altas›.

o: At the end of the sentence
why: Colors always follow the noun: ‹um carro preto›.
Adjectives in ‹-l› change to ‹-is› in the plural: ‹azuis›.
‹a gente› takes the ‹ele› form: ‹a gente fala›.
‹vocês› takes the ‹eles› form: ‹estudam›.
‹não› goes right before the verb, and ‹trabalho› is the ‹eu› form.
Where a person is takes ‹estar›, and the ‹eu› form is ‹estou›.

q: 'Where is the bank?' The usual Brazilian way:
why: For where a building is, Brazilians usually use ‹ficar›: ‹Onde fica o banco?›
How you are right now takes ‹estar›, and ‹cansada› agrees with the speaker, a woman.
‹em› + ‹a› always fuse into ‹na›, and ‹praia› is feminine.
‹o Brasil› takes the article, so ‹de› + ‹o› fuse into ‹do›.

q: Which city takes an article, so it contracts?
why: ‹o Rio› takes the article: ‹no Rio›, ‹do Rio›. Most cities take none.
A party is an event, and where an event takes place uses ‹ser›.
How you feel at the moment takes ‹estar›, and ‹nervoso› agrees with the speaker, a man.

o: She is from a pretty place.
why: With ‹estar›, ‹bonita› describes how she looks now; ‹Ela é bonita› describes the person.

q: How do you say I'm twenty (‹vinte›)?
why: Age uses ‹ter›: you have years. ‹Eu tenho vinte anos›.

q: In everyday Brazilian speech, how do you ask Is there a pharmacy near here?
why: In speech, ‹tem› means there is or there are.

q: How do you say I'm hungry?
why: Hunger is a noun in Portuguese: ‹estar com fome›, literally to be with hunger.

q: How do you ask Do you speak Portuguese?
why: Portuguese has no word for do: same order as the statement, with a rising voice.
‹porque›, one word, means because; ‹por que› and ‹por quê› ask why.

q: How many sisters do you have? =
why: ‹quanto› agrees with ‹irmãs›, which is feminine plural: ‹quantas›.
From two on the verb is plural (‹são›), and ‹hora› is feminine (‹duas›).

q: How is a price tag of R$ 30 read aloud?
why: R$ means ‹reais›, and the plural of ‹real› is ‹reais›.
‹um› agrees with a feminine noun: ‹vinte e uma pessoas›.
‹de› + ‹o› = ‹do›, and the contraction agrees with ‹banco›, which is masculine.

q: The keys are on the table. =
why: Movable things take ‹estar› (plural: ‹estão›), and ‹mesa› is feminine, so ‹da›.
‹de› + ‹a› = ‹da›: the contraction agrees with ‹farmácia›, which is feminine.

q: A woman talks about her father. She says…
why: The possessive agrees with the thing owned: ‹pai› is masculine, so ‹meu›.

q: Her car, said the clear Brazilian way =
why: Her = ‹dela›, after the noun; ‹o› agrees with ‹carro›.

q: Pointing at something you don't name: What's that?
why: For an unnamed thing, use ‹isso›; ‹esse› and ‹essa› need a noun after them.
‹fazer› is irregular in the ‹eu› form: ‹faço›.
The ‹nós› form of ‹ir› is ‹vamos›.

q: In a clothing store: Can I try it on? =
why: ‹Posso› (the ‹eu› form of ‹poder›) + the infinitive, with nothing in between.
‹ir› + the infinitive, with nothing between them: ‹vou viajar›.

q: We're going to have dinner at home. (use ‹a gente›)
why: ‹A gente› takes the ‹ele› form: ‹vai›, then the infinitive.
‹falarei› is the one-word future, mostly written; in conversation, ‹vou falar›.
‹gostar› always takes ‹de›: ‹gosto de café›.
‹de› + ‹a› = ‹da›, and ‹praia› is feminine.
‹adorar› goes straight to the thing: ‹adoro samba›, with no ‹de›.

q: How do you say 'I need help'?
why: ‹precisar› takes ‹de› before a noun: ‹Preciso de ajuda›.

q: How do you say 'I go by car'?
why: Vehicles take ‹de›, with no article: ‹de carro›, ‹de ônibus›.

q: 'Thanks for everything' (said by a man) is…
why: Thanks for is ‹obrigado por›; ‹para› is for where you are going or who gets something.

q: How do you say 'I'm studying right now'?
why: ‹estar› + the ‹-ndo› form: ‹estou estudando›.
‹-er› verbs drop the ‹r› and add ‹-ndo›: ‹comendo›.

q: Which one means 'I work at a bank' as a general fact, not right now?
why: For habits and facts, use the simple present; ‹estar› + ‹-ndo› is for what is happening now.

q: How do Brazilians say 'My name is Ana'?
why: In Brazil the pronoun goes before the verb, and ‹eu› takes ‹me›: ‹Eu me chamo Ana›.
‹A gente› takes the ‹ele› form, so ‹se›: ‹a gente se levanta›.

q: How does ‹Eu levanto às sete› (with no ‹me›) sound to a Brazilian?
why: Brazilians often drop the pronoun with routine verbs; both versions are fine.

q: Where does ‹me› go in ‹Você me ajuda›? (Can you help me?)
o: At the end of the sentence
why: In Brazil the short pronoun goes before the verb.

q: In everyday speech, 'I know her' is usually…
why: In speech ‹ela› goes after the verb; writing uses ‹Eu a conheço›.
Written ‹o› before a verb means him; it looks like the article but is not.
‹trabalhei› is the ‹eu› form of the ‹pretérito perfeito›.

q: How do you say 'Have you ever been to Brazil?'
why: For 'ever', use ‹já› + the ‹pretérito perfeito›: ‹Você já foi…?›

o: Both: a time word tells you which
why: The ‹nós› form of regular verbs is the same in the present and the past.

q: Which is the polite way to ask at a pharmacy?
why: ‹Eu queria› + ‹por favor› is the polite way to ask for something.

q: In Brazil, 'Can I have a coffee, please?' at a counter is usually…
why: In Brazil the pronoun comes first: ‹Me dá…?› (‹Dá-me› is the order used in Portugal.)

q: A stranger tells you ‹Vire à esquerda›. What do you do?
why: ‹esquerda› = left; ‹direita› = right.
Because is one word with no accent: ‹porque›.
‹mais› = more; ‹mas› = but.

q: 'I don't like tea.' 'Me neither.' Which reply fits?
why: Not either is ‹também não›.
‹à› = ‹a› + ‹a›, and it is always the feminine ‹direita›.
One bus takes ‹vai›, and ‹para› goes with the destination.

q: Which verb do Brazilians use most for catching a bus or an Uber?
why: ‹pegar› (catch) is the everyday verb: ‹pegar o ônibus›, ‹pegar um Uber›.
